newsitem.title: BULGARIA: BULGARIA PLANS LONGER TERM T-PAPER FOR DEBT SERVICE.
newsitem.headline: BULGARIA PLANS LONGER TERM T-PAPER FOR DEBT SERVICE.

text.p: The Bulgarian Finance Ministry plans to issue mainly longer-term government securities in the second half of this year in a bid to back payments on the domestic government debt, a Finance Ministry official said on Friday.

"The Finance Ministry plans to issue government securities with maturities falling in next years in order to meet the amount of domestic debt payments assumed in this year's budget draft," Plamen Oresharski, head of Finance Ministry State Treasury and Debt department, told Reuters.

The 1997 budget draft envisages interest payments on the government's domestic debt for this year at 6.9 percent of the projected gross domestic product (GDP) of 16.150 trillion levs, or around 1.114 trillion levs.

Oresharski said that the net bank financing of the budget deficit during this year will be negative, meaning that the funds collected through debt instruments will be less than the dues paid to financial institutions.

A minus 0.5 percent of net bank financing of the budget deficit was set in the 1997 budget draft as part of implementation of an IMF-prescribed currency board system which bans central bank lending to the government and banks.
Under the currency board system, to be launched on July 1, liquidity in the banking system will be regulated through the market of government securities and interbank deposits, said Oresharski.
Currently the Finance Ministry sustains banks' short-term liquidity through four-week discout treasury bills sold daily by the ministry.
High yields and expectations for low exchange rate risk under the currency board sytem attracted around $130 million investment in government paper from foreign investors in the past several months.
Oresharski said the four-week paper will probably be issued at least until the end of this year as their par value total will gradually be reduced to around 10 billion levs from 18 billion levs now.

In a bid to boost trade on the currently somnolent local secondary market the Finance Ministry plans to place fewer issues with higher par value, so that more institutions qualify in the auctions, said Oresharski.
"Instead of offering three of four issues with a total par value of some 30 billion levs in one day we may offer one issue with the same par," he added Oresharski.

In a bid to boost participation in primary auctions of more non-financial institutions like firms and individuals the ministry also plans to introduce a "per investor percentage of par limit" for non-competitive bids, he said.
Currently 30 percent of an issue's par value can be sold to non-financial institutions and frequently only one institution subscribes the whole amount.
The 1997 budget draft estimates that up to 1.6 percent of the budget deficit should be funded from non-financial institutions.
